prompt: From this model, which element(s) have an impact on how much money the customer spent?

options.text: Gender
Age
Social
Duration

explanation: Only coefficients with p < 0.05 are significant: gender (0.002), age (0.030) – and channel (0.004), which is not an option. Duration (0.567) and social (0.832) are not significant, so we cannot interpret them despite their large coefficients.

prompt: Disregarding age, what is the difference in spending between a male customer purchasing online and a female customer purchasing offline?

options.text: Female/offline spends 23.1 less
Male/online spends 12.7 more
Female/offline spends 35.8 more
Male/online spends 10.4 less

explanation: Male online: β0 − 23.1. Female offline: β0 + 12.7. Difference = 12.7 − (−23.1) = 35.8 in favour of female/offline.

prompt: A 24-year-old female customer who usually shops online, last bought 37 days ago and follows the brand on social media. What is her forecast transaction value?
explanation: Include only significant variables (plus the intercept): 52.3 + 12.7 (female) + 1.4 × 24 (= 33.6) − 23.1 (online) = 75.50 €. Duration and social are not significant and are left out.

prompt: What does the R² of 65% tell you?

options.text: The model explains 65% of the variance in transaction value
35% of the variance remains unexplained (error)
65% of the coefficients are significant
The forecast is correct for 65% of customers

explanation: R² = explained variance / total variance – an indication of how precise the predictions are.

prompt: For which purposes can regression analysis be used in marketing planning?

options.text: Marketing mix modelling – effectiveness of channels and campaigns
Budget optimisation – predict the impact of budget allocations
Sales forecasting
Price optimisation – predict willingness to pay from customer characteristics
Perceptual mapping of brands

explanation: Regression analyses relationships between a dependent and independent variables to explain and predict.

prompt: Which measurement scales can be used in traditional (linear) regression?

options.text: Metric (interval or ratio) dependent variable
Metric independent variables
Nominal independent variables transformed into binary (dummy) variables
Nominal dependent variable

explanation: The DV must be metric. Nominal IVs must be dummy-coded; ordinal variables are not used in traditional regression.

prompt: Package colour has three levels (red, yellow, green). How is it included as an independent variable?

options.text: Two dummy variables (red: 0/1, yellow: 0/1); green is the baseline when both are 0
One variable coded 1, 2, 3
Three dummy variables all included in the model
It cannot be included

explanation: k categories → k−1 dummies; the omitted category is the reference. Same in the start-up example: three states, two dummies, Florida as baseline.

prompt: Which are the four steps of a regression analysis (in order)?

options.text: Model formulation → estimation of the regression function → test of the regression function → test of the regression coefficients
Estimation → model formulation → test of coefficients → test of the function
Test of the function → estimation → formulation → test of coefficients
Data collection → clustering → profiling → targeting

explanation: Formulation (incl. checking linearity with scatter plots), estimation (OLS), test of the function (R², F), test of coefficients (t-test).

prompt: How does ordinary least squares (OLS) choose the regression line?

options.text: It minimises the sum of the squared residuals
It maximises R² by adding variables
It minimises the number of outliers
It sets the intercept to zero

explanation: Residual = observed − estimated value; OLS chooses b0, b1 so that Σ residuals² is minimal.

prompt: In a simple regression analysis, the intercept indicates …

options.text: the observed value of the dependent variable when the independent variable is zero
the estimated value of the dependent variable when the independent variable is zero
the estimated value of the independent variable when the dependent variable is zero
the observed value of the independent variable when the dependent variable is zero

explanation: The intercept is the ESTIMATED value of Y at X = 0 (recap quiz of session 10).

statement: Regression analysis is used both to explain relationships between variables and to predict values of the dependent variable.
explanation: Simple regression: one IV; multiple regression: several IVs.

statement: The selection of the dependent and independent variables must be based on conceptual or theoretical grounds.
explanation: Otherwise there is a danger of spurious correlations (e.g. ice cream sales and murders – both driven by the weather).

statement: Linear regression assumes a linear relationship between the dependent and each independent variable, which can be checked with scatter plots.
explanation: Linearity assumption.

statement: The slope coefficient indicates the change in the dependent variable due to a one-unit change in the independent variable.
explanation: E.g. one more salesman visit → +18.881 packages (simple regression).

statement: A residual is the difference between the observed and the estimated value of the dependent variable.
explanation: It expresses the impact of factors that are not / cannot be measured.

statement: R² can decrease when an additional independent variable is added to the model.
explanation: R² grows (or at least does not change) when IVs are added – even irrelevant ones. That is why the adjusted R² is used.

statement: R² is the proportion of explained variance in the dependent variable and ranges from 0 to 1.
explanation: Close to 1 = very good fit.

statement: The t-test of a regression coefficient tests H0: βj = 0.
explanation: If the true coefficient differs from 0, the IV has a significant influence.

statement: A coefficient is significant at the 5% level if its p-value is greater than 0.05.
explanation: Significant if p < 0.05 (|t_emp| > t_tab).

statement: The empirical t-value is the coefficient divided by its standard error.
explanation: t = b_j / SE(b_j); t-values can be negative.

statement: A non-significant coefficient should still be used to make predictions because its value is large.
explanation: Always check significance first; non-significant variables are not interpreted and left out of the forecast.

statement: If variables are measured in different units, the absolute size of their coefficients shows their relative importance.
explanation: Coefficients must be standardised to compare importance.

statement: The F-statistic assesses whether the regression model as a whole is useful for revealing the relationship in the population.
explanation: Together with R² it tests the regression function.

statement: In the margarine example, the simple regression predicts 39.534 packages for an area with zero salesman visits.
explanation: That is the intercept.

statement: In the monthly sales model, price has a significant negative effect on units sold.
explanation: Price's p-value is 0.130 > 0.05 → not significant.

statement: In the Adidas model, online purchases are associated with a lower transaction value than offline purchases.
explanation: Channel coefficient −23.1 (p = 0.004).

statement: In the Adidas model, social media followers spend 27.6 € more on average.
explanation: Social is not significant (p = 0.832), so this coefficient cannot be interpreted.

prompt: Forecast the transaction value of a 24-year-old female customer who shops online, last purchased 37 days ago and follows Adidas on social media. Explain which variables you include.
modelAnswer:
Only significant variables (p < 0.05) are included, plus the intercept: gender (0.002), age (0.030), channel (0.004). Duration and social are not significant and are left out.
Y = 52.3 + 12.7 × 1 + 1.4 × 24 − 23.1 × 1 = 52.3 + 12.7 + 33.6 − 23.1 = 75.50 €.

prompt: Explain the four steps of a regression analysis and what is tested in steps 3 and 4.
modelAnswer: 1 Model formulation: choose DV and IVs on theoretical grounds and check linearity (scatter plots). 2 Estimation: estimate the regression function with OLS (minimise the sum of squared residuals). 3 Test of the regression function: how well does the model fit – R² (explained/total variance), adjusted R², F-statistic. 4 Test of the coefficients: t-test of H0: βj = 0 for each IV – significant if |t| > t_tab or p < 0.05.
keyPoints: Test function: R², adjusted R², F

prompt: Interpret the regression results for monthly unit sales: model fit, significant variables and where to invest.
modelAnswer: The model fits very well (R² = 0.99, adjusted 0.98, F significant). SEM (0.472, p = 0.018), social media (1.380, p = 0.044) and the seasonal dummy (1,534.58, p = 0.000) are significant; price (p = 0.130) is not. Each extra € on social media is associated with ~1.38 more units, each € on SEM with ~0.47 units; the summer months sell ~1,535 more units. To increase sales, shift budget towards social media campaigns (while keeping the seasonal effect in mind).
keyPoints: Invest in social media (higher return per €)
